targetPath: /argentina/place/plaza-de-mulas/tour/
kind: destination_tours
status: approved
buttonLabel: "Explore tours via Plaza de Mulas"
lead: >-
  Plaza de Mulas is the base camp on the normal route to the summit of Aconcagua. The Ada Tours collection includes a 20-day expedition passing through the camp: an approach via the Horcones Valley, acclimatization, high-altitude camps and contingency time before a summit attempt. Discover why the expedition stops here, how it differs from a visit to Plaza Francia and what preparation the route requires.
---

## Which tour passes through Plaza de Mulas?

{{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} pass through [Plaza de Mulas base camp](/argentina/place/plaza-de-mulas/). Our selection includes the [20-day, 19-night “Aconcagua 6,962 m Climb”](/argentina/tour/aconcagua-climb/). The ultimate objective is the summit of [Aconcagua](/argentina/place/aconcagua/); Plaza de Mulas provides the base for preparing for the upper part of the ascent.

This route is for travelers seeking a full mountaineering expedition involving several camps and gradual adaptation to altitude. The itinerary includes rest days, practice climbs, carrying equipment to higher camps and reserve days. Having extra days does not guarantee a successful summit: the decision depends on the weather and the group's condition.

If you want to experience the Andes without attempting the summit, consider a trek to high-altitude viewpoints separately. Such a trip has a different duration, physical demands and permit requirements. **The current Ada Tours program in this selection is specifically a summit expedition**, not a short walk to base camp.

## How Plaza de Mulas fits into the 20-day expedition

The camp comes into the itinerary after the first acclimatization days. Participants begin in [Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/), pass Puente del Inca and reach [Confluencia camp](/argentina/place/confluencia/). From Confluencia, the group hikes to [Plaza Francia](/argentina/place/plaza-francia/) below Aconcagua's south face and returns to camp for the night. The next stage leads to Plaza de Mulas.

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| Confluencia | First camp and acclimatization |
| [Plaza Francia](/argentina/place/plaza-francia/) | Hike towards the south face |
| Plaza de Mulas | Base camp and rest |
| [Cerro Bonete](/argentina/place/cerro-bonete/) | Acclimatization hike |
| Camp Canadá | First higher-altitude stage |
| [Nido de Cóndores](/argentina/place/nido-de-condores/) | Continuing the ascent |

The transfer to Plaza de Mulas is scheduled for day 5. A rest day with crampon practice follows, then an ascent of Bonete, a practice climb towards Camp Canadá and another recovery day. Only then does the group proceed to the upper camps.

This sequence explains why **a 20-day expedition does not mean 20 consecutive days of climbing**. Some days are reserved for acclimatization, working with equipment and waiting for suitable conditions. The [full climbing itinerary](/argentina/tour/aconcagua-climb/) sets out every day's schedule, meals and equipment transport.

## Plaza de Mulas versus Plaza Francia

The names are similar, but the two places serve different purposes on this expedition.

[Plaza Francia](/argentina/place/plaza-francia/) is a destination for a hike towards Aconcagua's south face. The group walks there from Confluencia and returns to the same camp. The day's purpose is to see the face and acclimatize, not to continue climbing it.

[Plaza de Mulas](/argentina/place/plaza-de-mulas/) lies on the approach to the normal climbing route at approximately 4,300 m. This is where the expedition establishes its base camp, rests and prepares to climb higher. Overnight stays and practice ascents make this stop much more important to the onward expedition than a simple viewpoint.

When choosing a tour that includes either location, check the day-by-day itinerary. A reference to Plaza Francia does not necessarily mean the trip reaches Plaza de Mulas, just as reaching base camp does not guarantee participants will attempt the summit.

## What several days at base camp provide

At high altitude, familiar levels of exertion feel different. Plaza de Mulas sits above most cities and ski resorts. Walking pace, recovery after outings and sleep all become important parts of planning. Moving between higher camps must be gradual, while poor weather may disrupt the timetable.

On the [Aconcagua expedition](/argentina/tour/aconcagua-climb/), days around base camp have different purposes: resting after the approach, practicing with crampons, climbing [Bonete](/argentina/place/cerro-bonete/) and carrying equipment towards Camp Canadá. These are distinct activities, not identical days of free time.

Mules carry some personal belongings during the approach. The arrangements change higher up: participants carry part of their own equipment, while porters may transport some group supplies. **The precise amount of assistance and the equipment provided must be checked in the conditions of the individual tour.**

For an independent trek to base camp, compare a different set of details: walking duration, overnight accommodation, guiding arrangements and permits for the intended activity. Conditions from a major mountaineering expedition cannot automatically be applied to a trekking trip.

## Who should choose a trip via Plaza de Mulas?

Choose this tour if your goal is to attempt Aconcagua's summit with proper preparation at altitude. It requires good physical fitness, the ability to walk for hours, tolerance of cold and readiness for life in tents. Altitude acclimatization is essential even for experienced athletes.

For a first encounter with the Andes without a mountaineering objective, start with the [Aconcagua guide](/argentina/place/aconcagua/) and compare [tours of Argentina](/argentina/tour/). Most ordinary sightseeing trips have very different requirements from a route via Plaza de Mulas.

If mountain preparation is your priority, compare not just the total trip length, but also the distribution of acclimatization hikes, the number of high-altitude camps, weather contingency days, medical requirements and baggage transport arrangements.

## Permits, season and safety

Aconcagua lies in Mendoza Province, within the provincial park of the same name. Treks involving overnight stays and summit expeditions have different permits and requirements. Park authorities regulate routes, visiting periods and medical checks; current rules should be confirmed before departure.

**Access to Plaza de Mulas is not the same as unrestricted entry to a short tourist trail.** You need a permit appropriate to the type of trip. Long hikes, altitude and the risk of sudden weather changes require carefully chosen equipment and experience with mountain exertion.

The best period for mountaineering programs generally corresponds to the operating season of the park's high-altitude infrastructure, usually the Southern Hemisphere summer. However, the opening of particular routes and admission rules may change. Check the park's current announcements and the terms of your chosen expedition.

## Frequently asked questions about tours via Plaza de Mulas

### Do I have to climb the summit to see base camp?

No. Plaza de Mulas can be the destination of a separate multiday trek. However, the [20-day Ada Tours program](/argentina/tour/aconcagua-climb/) is designed as an expedition with a summit attempt, so it cannot be treated as an off-the-shelf short trek without changes.

### How many days does the group spend around Plaza de Mulas?

The expedition reaches the camp on day 5. Rest days, acclimatization hikes and excursions involving returns to base camp follow. The timing of the later ascent depends on the full itinerary and actual conditions.

### Which is higher: Plaza Francia or Plaza de Mulas?

Both are in high mountain terrain at roughly 4,000 m. Different altitude figures appear in route descriptions depending on the exact location. For choosing a trip, the role of each stop matters more: the hike to [Plaza Francia](/argentina/place/plaza-francia/) starts from Confluencia, while Plaza de Mulas becomes the base for the next stage of the climb.

### Do I need a separate park permit?

Yes. Visiting the relevant trekking and mountaineering areas requires a permit issued under park regulations. The type depends on the route, overnight stays and activity. Compare the requirements of your tour with the rules in force on your travel dates.

### Does the itinerary guarantee reaching Aconcagua's summit?

No. Acclimatization and reserve days provide additional time, but cannot remove the effects of altitude, weather and health. Taking part in the expedition and reaching the summit are different outcomes.

kind: destination

buttonLabel: "Learn more about Congress Square and the Monument to the Two Congresses"
lead: >-
  Plaza del Congreso in Buenos Aires stands in front of the Argentine parliament building. Its principal landmark, the Monument to the Two Congresses, commemorates major events of 1813 and 1816. It makes a rewarding stop on a walk through the historic center, where architecture helps explain the country's struggle for independence.
---

## Congress Square in Buenos Aires: what the main monument represents

**Congress Square (Plaza del Congreso) is a historic public space in [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/)** opposite the Argentine National Congress building. Visit for its large sculptural ensemble and fountains, an unobstructed view of the parliament building and an introduction to the country's history.

The square was designed by French landscape architect **Carlos Thays**. It opened in connection with the centenary of the May Revolution of 1810. Nearby green spaces form a sequence of public areas along the surrounding streets.

## Monument to the Two Congresses: 1813 and 1816

The main monument was inaugurated on **July 9, 1914**. Belgian sculptor **Jules Lagae** created the statues, while **Eugène D'Huicque** designed the architectural elements. The Republic is represented in the center, flanked by allegorical female figures commemorating two major events.

**The Assembly of 1813** is associated with reforms during the independence struggle and the development of national symbols. **The Congress of Tucumán in 1816** declared the independence of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata. The monument brings these events together as pivotal stages in the nation's history.

The fountain in front of the sculptures represents the Río de la Plata, while other allegorical figures symbolize the Paraná and Uruguay rivers. This is why the monument is best appreciated by walking around it rather than looking from a single viewpoint.

## What to look for on a visit

Begin at a position where you can see the Congress building and the monument together. This reveals the intended arrangement of the public space: a memorial standing before the parliament evokes the history and development of state institutions.

Then approach the fountain ensemble, examine the figures and reliefs and walk through the green spaces. The square also contains a marker for **kilometer zero of Argentina's national road network**, a small but interesting reference point for anyone curious about the country's geography and infrastructure.

| Landmark | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Monument to the Two Congresses | Independence and reforms |
| Congress Palace | Parliamentary government |
| Fountain | Rivers of the Río de la Plata basin |
| Kilometer zero | The geography of Argentina's roads |

Because it remains an active public space, parts of the square may occasionally close during political events, demonstrations and state occasions. Take the local situation into account when planning a visit.

## Congress Square and the Congress Palace are different attractions

**The open square is accessible as an urban public space**, while entering the National Congress building is subject to separate visitor or government arrangements. When booking a tour, check whether the itinerary includes only the exterior or a prearranged visit inside.

The parliament building is also of interest for its architecture and history. Its great dome and imposing facade are clearly visible from the square. A substantial guided visit should allow time to learn about the country's political institutions rather than just take a photograph beside the monument.

## Combining Congress Square with other sights

For a walk focusing on Argentina's political history, it makes sense to connect Congress Square with [Plaza de Mayo](/argentina/place/plaza-de-mayo/) and [Casa Rosada](/argentina/place/casa-rosada/). The historic avenue **Avenida de Mayo** runs between them and is known for facades dating from the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Along the way, you can see different periods of the city's history: the presidential palace and old square, the grand avenue and finally the National Congress. This route suits visitors who want to understand the capital and the nation's history, not merely see its best-known photo spots.

Congress Square is among the attractions on our [“Ice, Sun and the End of the Earth” itinerary](/multi-country/tour/argentina-brazil-private-tour-12-days/). Check how much time the schedule provides: a quick look at the facades and a full historical account offer different experiences.

## Frequently asked questions about Congress Square

### Where is Congress Square?

In front of the National Congress building in Buenos Aires, near the intersection of Rivadavia and Entre Ríos avenues.

### What does “Two Congresses” refer to?

The name refers to the Assembly of 1813 and the Congress of Tucumán of 1816, both associated with independence and the formation of the Argentine state.

### When was the main monument unveiled?

**July 9, 1914.** The square itself had been developed earlier for the centenary of the May Revolution.

### Can I enter the Congress building while visiting the square?

Access to the interior is governed by separate rules. A tour of the square and the parliament's exterior does not automatically include an interior visit.

buttonLabel: "Discover Plaza Dorrego"
lead: >-
  Plaza Dorrego is a historic square in San Telmo, home to a famous antiques fair on Sundays. Old city houses, cafes and shops selling collectibles line its edges. Explore the square's history, its market and a convenient walking route through the neighborhood.
---

## Plaza Dorrego in San Telmo: an antiques fair and a historic square

Plaza Dorrego is a small square in the historic [San Telmo](/argentina/place/san-telmo/) neighborhood of [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/). Old buildings, cafes and antique shops surround it. Compared with the expansive [Plaza de Mayo](/argentina/place/plaza-de-mayo/), it feels more intimate and closer to the everyday life of the old city.

The square is best known for its Sunday antiques fair. It is also worth visiting on other days: nineteenth-century architecture survives around it, local businesses stay open, and the square provides a convenient stop while walking along Defensa Street.

## Why Plaza Dorrego is a historic site

In colonial times, this part of San Telmo was known as Alto de las Carretas, a stopping point for carts traveling towards the city center. The area later developed into a densely built urban neighborhood.

Plaza Dorrego is connected with a significant episode in Argentine history. In September 1816, the people of Buenos Aires were informed here of the independence proclaimed on July 9 that year by the Congress of Tucumán. This event should not be confused with the May Revolution of 1810, associated with the capital's principal square.

Today Plaza Dorrego is recognized as a National Historic Monument. For travelers, both its historical significance and the preserved setting of the old neighborhood are part of its appeal.

## The San Telmo Sunday fair

On Sundays, Plaza Dorrego hosts the Feria de San Telmo, one of Buenos Aires' best-known antiques markets. It began in 1970 on the initiative of the city's Museo de la Ciudad. Over time, the stalls spread into neighboring streets.

Antiques have traditionally dominated the square itself, while Defensa and nearby streets offer more handicrafts, souvenirs and works by contemporary makers. Merchandise and prices vary between vendors.

| When to visit | What to expect |
|---|---|
| Sunday | The fair and larger crowds |
| Weekday | A quieter square |
| Evening | Cafes, subject to individual opening hours |

Tango is also associated with the square's Sunday activities. The city tourist portal describes a “Patio de Tango” here, but no particular performer or performance time can be guaranteed on any given Sunday.

## What to see around the square

Plaza Dorrego is a few minutes' walk from Defensa Street, San Telmo's main walking route. Follow it to the historic market, first opened in 1897, where food stalls and fresh produce now share space with traders in vintage objects.

Nearby are old mansions with inner courtyards and antique shops. Some welcome visitors as galleries, while others still serve residential or commercial purposes. Walking without a rigid list of dozens of stops allows time to admire facades and enter places that catch your interest.

The square itself is small, so a visit without the fair does not take long. Its greatest attraction is its connection with the rest of San Telmo.

## Adding Plaza Dorrego to a trip

A logical walking route starts at [Plaza de Mayo](/argentina/place/plaza-de-mayo/), continues along Defensa Street and passes San Telmo Market before reaching Plaza Dorrego. This connects sites associated with the country's political history to the everyday streets of old Buenos Aires.

Some of our [Argentina tours](/argentina/tour/) include a capital-city sightseeing excursion through San Telmo. For example, [“Best of Argentina: 14 Days”](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-14-days/) introduces visitors to Buenos Aires neighborhoods before the trip continues elsewhere in the country.

If the Sunday fair is the main attraction for you, check the day of the week in the tour schedule. Mentioning San Telmo on an itinerary does not mean the fair will be visited when it is not operating.

## Tips for visiting

Morning or the first half of the day is a good time to visit the fair. Popular Sundays can be crowded, and stretches of Defensa become largely pedestrian. Wear comfortable shoes and look after your belongings.

When buying expensive antiques, discuss authenticity and documentation directly with the seller; an object that looks old does not necessarily have a documented history. If you are mainly interested in photographs of the architecture and visits to cafes, a weekday may be more enjoyable.

## Frequently asked questions about Plaza Dorrego

### Where is Plaza Dorrego?

In the San Telmo neighborhood of Buenos Aires, close to Defensa Street.

### On which day is the fair held?

On Sundays. It takes place in the square and adjacent streets, but precise arrangements depend on city scheduling and the calendar.

### Is it true that Argentina's independence was announced here?

Yes. In September 1816, residents of the capital were informed here of independence proclaimed by the Congress of Tucumán.

### Can I visit the square on weekdays?

Yes. The square and the surrounding old houses are of interest throughout the year, although the Sunday fair does not take place on an ordinary weekday.

## Tours visiting Plaza Dorrego in Buenos Aires

[Plaza Dorrego](/argentina/place/plaza-dorrego/) is in [San Telmo](/argentina/place/san-telmo/), one of the oldest neighborhoods of [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/). It is usually visited during a city tour alongside La Boca, Plaza de Mayo and other historic districts. You do not need an entire day here, but even a brief stop reveals a side of Buenos Aires beyond its grand avenues.

Our catalog features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} that include the square in their main itinerary. They differ chiefly in **overall trip duration, countries visited and the format of the Buenos Aires sightseeing day**. A stop at Plaza Dorrego does not automatically mean that a trip is timed to coincide with the Sunday fair.

| Tour | Main difference |
|---|---|
| [Argentina and Patagonia, 26 days](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/) | Extended route across Argentina and neighboring countries |
| [5 countries in 18 days](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) | Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Bolivia and Peru |
| [Chile and Argentina, 17 days](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-private-grand-tour-17-days/) | Private grand tour including Iguazu |
| [Best of Argentina, 14 days](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-14-days/) | Buenos Aires, Patagonia, Bariloche and Iguazu |
| [New Year's Fairy Tale, 11 days](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-new-year-11-days-2027/) | Festive journey through three countries |
| [Parade of Champions, 10 days](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-champions-parade-10-days-2027/) | Carnival, tango and wine experiences |

The table helps you choose the **type of overall journey**. For the visit to the square itself, it is more useful to read the Buenos Aires day carefully: which districts are listed, whether a guide is provided, what happens in the evening and whether there is any free time.

## How Plaza Dorrego fits into a city tour

A typical city route connects [La Boca](/argentina/place/la-boca/), [San Telmo](/argentina/place/san-telmo/), Plaza Dorrego, [Plaza de Mayo](/argentina/place/plaza-de-mayo/) and [Casa Rosada](/argentina/place/casa-rosada/). Along the way, visitors see contrasting sides of the capital: colorful houses in the former port district, narrow historic streets, the country's political center and modern thoroughfares.

On the [14-day “Best of Argentina” tour](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-14-days/), day 2 includes a private sightseeing tour with a Russian-speaking guide. Plaza Dorrego and other historic sights are explicitly listed. An evening tango show with dinner is also included as a separate itinerary item, not as an automatic part of the square visit.

The [17-day private grand tour of Chile and Argentina](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-private-grand-tour-17-days/) devotes day 16 to Buenos Aires. It includes San Telmo and Plaza Dorrego, [Recoleta](/argentina/place/recoleta/), [Recoleta Cemetery](/argentina/place/recoleta-cemetery/) and Puerto Madero. An evening tango show with dinner is also described. Travelers wanting to see more city districts in one day will find this quite different from a short San Telmo-only stroll.

On the [10-day Parade of Champions itinerary](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-champions-parade-10-days-2027/), the city tour lasts three hours with a Russian-speaking guide; San Telmo and Plaza Dorrego are on the list of stops. This is a short introduction to several neighborhoods, so time spent at the square depends on the schedule of the entire sightseeing day.

Ada Tours also offers a [private excursion through the historic districts](/argentina/buenos-aires/buenos-aires-historic-districts-russian-private/) and a [three-hour group sightseeing tour](/argentina/buenos-aires/buenos-aires-three-hours-russian-group/). Read their conditions separately: the existence of a standalone excursion does not mean that every multiday trip includes that precise version.

## Which multiday trip should you choose?

**If Argentina is your main destination**, compare the [14-day journey including Bariloche and Iguazu](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-14-days/) with the [26-day Argentina and Patagonia program](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/). Both include historic Buenos Aires neighborhoods, but the rest of their routes differ considerably in scope. The longer trip covers more regions and natural areas, while the shorter one offers a tighter selection of famous places.

**If you want to visit several countries during one vacation**, consider the [18-day “5 Countries of Latin America” itinerary](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/). Buenos Aires is one stage alongside Brazil, Chile, Bolivia and Peru. Travelers choose this option for its geographical variety while accepting the need for several overland transfers and flights.

The [17-day private grand tour](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-private-grand-tour-17-days/) combines Chile, Argentina and Iguazu Falls in Brazil. Its day in Buenos Aires comes towards the end of the longer journey. The itinerary suits travelers interested in both the landscapes of the continent's south and a guided introduction to Buenos Aires without arranging a separate city trip.

The [New Year's tour through Brazil, Argentina and Chile](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-new-year-11-days-2027/) and [“Parade of Champions, Tango and Wine”](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-champions-parade-10-days-2027/) are chosen for a different reason: their travel themes are linked to celebrations. Plaza Dorrego is included as a city experience, but the specific festive activities take place in other parts of the route. Check the tour's dates against the event calendar.

## The Sunday fair versus an ordinary day

Plaza Dorrego is chiefly known for its Sunday antiques fair. Stalls fill the square and extend along Defensa Street. Visitors search for old books, records, furniture, household objects and collectibles. Cafes and antique shops operate around the square.

On other days, the square is quieter: you can see the historic buildings, sit in a cafe and walk through neighboring streets. That experience is available even when there is no fair. Tango music and street performances are often associated with San Telmo, but **a particular performance cannot be promised on any day at any time**.

If the Sunday market is the main reason for your trip, check which day you will spend in Buenos Aires. Ada Tours' multiday itineraries list the square as a sightseeing stop, but a reference to it does not confirm a market visit during opening hours.

The square's historical importance extends beyond trading. In September 1816, the independence proclaimed several months earlier in Tucumán was announced here to the people of Buenos Aires. Historical accounts of the city commemorate that event, while the square remains a lively public space today.

## What else to see near Plaza Dorrego

A historical walk through San Telmo naturally continues along Defensa Street. Browse antique shop windows before visiting other sights around Buenos Aires. The following stops are particularly suitable for exploring the old city:

- [San Telmo](/argentina/place/san-telmo/) — old streets, cafes and antique shops.
- [La Boca](/argentina/place/la-boca/) — a colorful neighborhood with a distinctive port history.
- [Plaza de Mayo](/argentina/place/plaza-de-mayo/) — the capital's historic and political heart.
- [Casa Rosada](/argentina/place/casa-rosada/) — the recognizable building beside the central square.
- [Recoleta](/argentina/place/recoleta/) and [its historic cemetery](/argentina/place/recoleta-cemetery/) — another district with very different architecture and atmosphere.

These places occur in different combinations on city tours. If sightseeing independently, organizing your route by neighborhood makes more sense than trying to cross the entire city to visit every site simply because they appear in one itinerary.

[Argentina tours](/argentina/tour/) and [cultural journeys through Argentina](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/argentina/) offer other combinations of city visits and natural regions. Plaza Dorrego is just one stop, so compare trips by their full itineraries.

## What to check before choosing a tour

First decide what you want from Buenos Aires: a brief sightseeing introduction, a longer walk through historic neighborhoods, free time for the market or an evening tango show. Then open the relevant day's program and check its length, guiding arrangements, included activities and time spent in the city.

**Access to the square and participation in an organized excursion are different things.** You can visit the open public space independently, but a guide, transport, restaurant or performance is included only when specified in the tour conditions. Do not assume that all city experiences are free or automatically included in the price of a longer trip.

When comparing multiday itineraries, remember that your time in Buenos Aires may be constrained by arrival, departure or a flight to the next region. A 26-day tour does not necessarily give you more free time at Plaza Dorrego than a 14-day tour; the actual city schedule determines that.

## Frequently asked questions about tours via Plaza Dorrego

### Is Plaza Dorrego in central Buenos Aires?

It is in the historic San Telmo neighborhood, south of the most central districts. It fits well into a city tour alongside La Boca and Plaza de Mayo. For a separate visit, allow time to explore neighboring streets.

### Which Ada Tours trips visit the square?

The selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. Examples are the [14-day journey through Argentina](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-14-days/), [18-day five-country tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) and [17-day private grand tour](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-private-grand-tour-17-days/), as well as other multiday programs.

### Can I visit the Sunday fair during a tour?

Only if the dates and time in Buenos Aires coincide with the fair and the sightseeing schedule allows a stop. Plaza Dorrego being listed on an itinerary does not guarantee a market visit.

### Is a tango show included in a visit to Plaza Dorrego?

No. It is a separate activity. Some tours offer an evening [tango show with dinner](/argentina/buenos-aires/buenos-aires-tango-show-with-dinner/) independently of the city tour; check the services and conditions of your chosen itinerary.

### How do I choose between a shorter and longer itinerary with this stop?

Consider the other countries and regions, the time allowed in Buenos Aires and the guiding arrangements. A city tour is enough to become acquainted with the square; additional days on longer journeys are primarily devoted to other experiences.

buttonLabel: "Learn more about the trek to Plaza Francia"
lead: >-
  Plaza Francia offers views of Aconcagua's south face: sheer rock, snow and glaciers rising above a dry high-altitude valley. Hikers approach from Confluencia camp for the panorama and for acclimatization. Discover the difficulty of the route, how the destination differs from Plaza de Mulas and its place in Ada Tours' current expedition itinerary.
---

## Plaza Francia: a view of Aconcagua's south face

Plaza Francia is in [Aconcagua](/argentina/place/aconcagua/) Provincial Park in Argentina's Mendoza Province. On most trekking routes, the name refers to the approach area and viewpoint at the foot of the mountain's south face. From here, enormous rock faces, snow and glaciers appear quite different from the distant views available from the main road.

Aconcagua's south face is known for demanding technical climbing routes. A hike to its base, however, has **a different objective**. Hikers wishing to see the wall up close do not need to begin a technical ascent on ice and rock.

Many reach Plaza Francia from [Confluencia](/argentina/place/confluencia/) on a day hike and return to camp afterwards. This allows travelers to experience the high mountains and gradually expose their bodies to greater exertion without moving camp every night.

## What the trek to Plaza Francia involves

A typical itinerary begins by entering the park through the Horcones Valley and walking to [Confluencia camp](/argentina/place/confluencia/). The next stage follows a rocky valley towards Aconcagua's south face. Vegetation becomes sparser, and the exposed mountain landscape grows more apparent.

The route reaches approximately 4,000 m or more, depending on the chosen endpoint. Participants spend many hours walking over rocks, potentially under intense sun or in strong winds. Even without ropes and technical climbing, the outing can be physically demanding.

Official information from Mendoza Province describes a three-day option: enter via Horcones, spend the night at Confluencia, then hike to the viewpoint or Plaza Francia and return to the same camp. Participants leave the park on the following day. This illustrates a trekking itinerary, not a fixed timetable for every season.

## Plaza Francia and Plaza de Mulas: the differences

| Place | Main purpose |
|---|---|
| Plaza Francia | Panorama of the south face and acclimatization |

[Plaza de Mulas](/argentina/place/plaza-de-mulas/) lies along a different part of the valley and serves as a base for expeditions following the normal route to the summit. Plaza Francia is primarily a destination for viewing the south face, and participants in multiday treks often return to Confluencia afterwards.

Visiting these two places does not mean travelers are undertaking a technical ascent of the south face itself. A mountaineering climb requires a different level of experience, equipment and type of permit.

If scenic views without a multiday hike are your main goal, start with the shorter visitor routes in [Aconcagua](/argentina/place/aconcagua/) Provincial Park. Plaza Francia demands far more effort than an ordinary walk near the entrance.

## Plaza Francia on the Ada Tours expedition

On the [20-day Aconcagua climbing itinerary](/argentina/tour/aconcagua-climb/), Plaza Francia is visited on day 4. After a night at Confluencia, participants walk to the foot of the south face, stop to acclimatize and return to the same camp after an afternoon snack. The next stage takes the group towards [Plaza de Mulas](/argentina/place/plaza-de-mulas/).

On this program, the walk towards the south face is preparation for the climb. Participants become accustomed to greater altitude before continuing. The day is also valuable in its own right for people interested in Andean landscapes, even if the summit attempt later proves impossible.

When planning, check the tour's specific conditions: permits, supporting team, meals, baggage handling and the number of contingency days. Terms for a full summit expedition cannot automatically be applied to a shorter trekking excursion.

## Weather, physical demands and permits

Exposed terrain beneath the south face can be windy, cold and intensely sunny. Low humidity and altitude make hydration and a measured walking pace especially important. Mountain weather can change abruptly; a guide may alter or cancel a hike if conditions are unfavorable.

Before setting out, ask the park authority whether the specific sector is open and what permit is required. High-altitude areas should not be approached independently without sufficient experience, appropriate equipment and a well-planned return. Permitted route operating periods differ by season and activity.

Protect the natural environment by staying on approved trails, carrying out rubbish and keeping clear of dangerous areas near glaciers. Good views of the south face are available from safe viewpoints; approaching icefalls is not a necessary part of a visitor's trip.

## Frequently asked questions about Plaza Francia

### Do I need to be a mountaineer to see Aconcagua's south face?

An organized trek to the viewpoint does not require a technical climbing ascent. The route is nevertheless at high altitude and demands good fitness, an appropriate permit and attention to the weather.

### Where do hikers stay overnight when visiting Plaza Francia?

On a common trekking itinerary, hikers stay at [Confluencia](/argentina/place/confluencia/), and the walk towards the face and back occupies a separate hiking day.

### Can I go straight from Plaza Francia to the summit?

Routes up the south face involve highly technical mountaineering. On our standard expedition, Plaza Francia is an acclimatization outing, after which the itinerary continues via [Plaza de Mulas](/argentina/place/plaza-de-mulas/).

### How much time should I allow for the trip?

This is not an ordinary stop on a bus tour. Options involving Confluencia take several days or require a carefully planned special itinerary depending on permits and participants' preparation.
